## PMM probabilities vs. most likely class

```{r}
analysis2_marginal_matching |>
  gt::gt(rowname_col = "method") |>
  gt::tab_spanner("Weighted %", columns = c(Normal, MCI, Dementia)) |>
  gt::tab_spanner("Difference from Manly-Jones (points)", columns = c(normal_gap, mci_gap, dementia_gap)) |>
  gt::cols_label(normal_gap = "Normal", mci_gap = "MCI", dementia_gap = "Dementia") |>
  gt::fmt_number(columns = c(Normal, MCI, Dementia), decimals = 1) |>
  gt::fmt_number(columns = c(normal_gap, mci_gap, dementia_gap), decimals = 2) |>
  gt::cols_align("center", columns = -method) |>
  a2_2_gt_style(font = 22, width = 95)
```

<div style="font-size: 0.5em; line-height: 1.25;">

- Averaging the PMM probabilities reproduces the Manly-Jones class rates, because the model was calibrated to them.
- Taking each person's most likely class does not. A person with probabilities of 0.55 Normal and 0.45 MCI counts as fully Normal. MCI carries a large share of the total probability but is rarely any one person's most likely class, so MCI shrinks and Normal grows.
- Use the probabilities for prevalence and the most likely class only where a single label is needed.

</div>
